chunks: Drawing an I2C bus connection. The question: How do I make the connections? Draw it out.
To draw an I2C bus, put the controller on one side with two pins, SCL and SDA.
Run two straight lines from those pins to every other chip, connecting SCL to SCL and SDA to SDA, straight through (unlike UART, where one chip's send pin goes to the other's receive pin).
At one point, add one resistor from each line up to the supply, called a pull-up. Tie all grounds together, and strap address pins so no two chips share an address.
Imagine two shared water pipes, each fed from a supply tank through a thin tap. Any device can open a valve to a drain and pull its pipe empty.
A pipe is full only when every valve is closed, and the thin tap refills it. That is a pull-up resistor and open-drain outputs.
Nobody pushes water in, so no two devices can fight. The taps appear once for the whole bus.
SCL and SDA run straight from the master to every slave, with a dot at each tap. The only resistors are the two pull-ups on the right, drawn once.
The lines cross where a slave's SCL tap goes down through the SDA line; a crossing without a dot is not a connection.
SCL and SDA: the shared clock line and data line. Each connects to the same-named pin on every chip.
Pull-up resistor: one resistor per line, to the supply, that makes the line high when nobody pulls it low ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Open-drain: an output that can only pull the line low ("Advantages of open-drain outputs"). Common ground: all chips share one ground.
Without it, voltages on the lines mean nothing. Address strap: tying an address pin to supply or ground to choose the chip's address.
Draw a controller, two sensors, and two lines. Sensor A has its address pin tied to ground, giving address 0x48 (hexadecimal), and sensor B has it tied to supply, giving 0x49.
Add one 2. 2 kilohms resistor from each line to 3. 3 volts. With about 100 picofarads of bus capacitance, the rise time is 0.
85 times 2200 times 100 picofarads about 186 nanoseconds, under the 300 nanoseconds limit for 400 kilohertz. That is the whole idea.
"I draw the master, then two shared lines, SCL and SDA, running to every slave, straight through with no crossover.
At one point on the bus I add one pull-up resistor from each line to the supply, around 2. 2 to 4. 7 kilohms at 3. 3 volts.
Grounds are tied together, every chip gets a decoupling cap, and address pins are strapped so no two slaves collide.
The pull-ups matter because every driver is open-drain, so it can only pull low."
